 *
 * This file is shipped INTO the sandbox by the orchestrator and executed there as
 * `node __agent_eval__/run.mjs '<AgentRunInput JSON>'`. It is intentionally

 *
 * The pure helpers below are exported (not just `runAgent`) so they can be
 * unit-tested directly — the same code the sandbox runs (see opencode.test.ts).
 */

import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';

This optimizes how Next.js prefetches and caches navigation data: 00554| 00555| - **Layout deduplication**: When prefetching multiple URLs with a shared layout, the layout is downloaded once. 00556| - **Incremental prefetching**: Next.js only prefetches parts not already in cache, rather than entire pages. 00557| 00558| These changes require **no code modifications** and are designed to improve performance across all apps. 00559| 00560| However, you may see more individual prefetch requests with much lower total transfer sizes. Run the latest upgrade CLI from your app's directory:

```bash filename="Terminal"
npx next@canary upgrade --agent=latest

The CLI prepares the Next.js 16 migration guides and codemod command for the agent, then asks it to apply the changes and verify the app. See [Upgrade with a coding agent](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/agent-upgrade) for details.

See [Version-matched documentation](/docs/app/guides/ai-agents#version-matched-documentation) for the managed block and setup details. 00037| 00038| ## Using the codemod 00039| 00040| To update to Next.js version 16, you can use the `upgrade` [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/codemods#160): 00041| 00042| ```bash package="pnpm" 00043| pnpm dlx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest 00044| ``` 00045| 00046| ```bash package="npm" 00047| npx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest 00048| ``` 00049| 00050| ```bash package="yarn" 00051| yarn dlx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest 00052| ``` 00053| 00054| ```bash package="bun" 00055| bunx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest 00056| ``` 00057| 00058| The [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/codemods#160) is able to: 00059| 00060| - Update `next.config.js` to use the new `turbopack` configuration 00061| - Migrate from `next lint` to the ESLint CLI 00062| - Migrate from deprecated `middleware` convention to `proxy` 00063| - Remove `unstable_` prefix from stabilized APIs 00064| - Remove `experimental_ppr` Route Segment Config from pages and layouts 00065| 00066| The `upgrade` codemod does not run every migration codemod. If your app still uses synchronous `params`, `searchParams`, `cookies()`, `headers()`, or `draftMode()` access from the Next.js 15 compatibility period, also run the async Request APIs codemod: 00067| 00068| ```bash filename="Terminal" 00069| npx @next/codemod@canary next-async-request-api . 00070| ``` 00071| 00072| ## Install packages manually 00073| 00074| If you prefer to do it manually, install the latest Next.js and React versions: 00075| 00076| ```bash package="pnpm" 00077| pnpm add next@latest react@latest react-dom@latest 00078| ``` 00079| 00080| ```bash package="npm" 00081| npm install next@latest react@latest react-dom@latest 00082| ``` 00083| 00084| ```bash package="yarn" 00085| yarn add next@latest react@latest react-dom@latest 00086| ``` 00087| 00088| ```bash package="bun" 00089| bun add next@latest react@latest react-dom@latest 00090| ``` 00091| 00092| If you are using TypeScript, ensure you also upgrade `@types/react` and `@types/react-dom` to their latest versions. 00093| 00094| ## Node.js runtime and browser support 00095| 00096| | Requirement | Change / Details | 00097| | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | 00098| | Node.js 20.9+ | Minimum version now `20.9.0` (LTS); Node.js 18 no longer supported | 00099| | TypeScript 5+ | Minimum version now `5.1.0` | 00100| | Browsers | Chrome 111+, Edge 111+, Firefox 111+, Safari 16.4+ | 00101| 00102| ## Turbopack by default 00103| 00104| Starting with **Next.js 16**, Turbopack is stable and used by default with `next dev` and `next build` 00105| 00106| Previously you had to enable Turbopack using `--turbopack`, or `--turbo`. 00107| 00108| ```json filename="package.json" 00109| { 00110| "scripts": { 00111| "dev": "next dev --turbopack", 00112| "build": "next build --turbopack", 00113| "start": "next start" 00114| } 00115| } 00116| ``` 00117| 00118| This is no longer necessary. You can update your `package.json` scripts: 00119| 00120| ```json filename="package.json" 00121| { 00122| "scripts": { 00123| "dev": "next dev", 00124| "build": "next build", 00125| "start": "next start" 00126| } 00127| } 00128| ``` 00129| 00130| If your project has a [custom `webpack`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/webpack) configuration and you run `next build` (which now uses Turbopack by default), the build will **fail** to prevent misconfiguration issues. 00131| 00132| You have a few different ways to address this: 00133| 00134| - **Use Turbopack anyway:** Run with `next build --turbopack` to build using Turbopack and ignore your `webpack` config. 00135| - **Switch to Turbopack fully:** Migrate your `webpack` config to Turbopack-compatible options. 00136| - **Keep using Webpack:** Use the `--webpack` flag to opt out of Turbopack and build with Webpack. 00137| 00138| > **Good to know**: If you see failing builds because a `webpack` configuration was found, but you don't define one yourself, it is likely that a plugin is adding a `webpack` option 00139| 00140| ### Opting out of Turbopack 00141| 00142| If you need to continue using Webpack, you can opt out with the `--webpack` flag. For example, to use Turbopack in development but Webpack for production builds: 00143| 00144| ```json filename="package.json" 00145| { 00146| "scripts": { 00147| "dev": "next dev", 00148| "build": "next build --webpack", 00149| "start": "next start" 00150| } 00151| } 00152| ``` 00153| 00154| We recommend using Turbopack for development and production. Submit a comment to this [thread](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/77721), if you are unable to switch to Turbopack. 00155| 00156| ### Turbopack configuration location 00157| 00158| The `experimental.turbopack` configuration is out of experimental. 00159| 00160| ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 00161| import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 00162| 00163| // Next.js 15 - experimental.turbopack 00164| const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 00165| experimental: { 00166| turbopack: { 00167| // options 00168| }, 00169| }, 00170| } 00171| 00172| export default nextConfig 00173| ``` 00174| 00175| You can use it as a top-level `turbopack` option: 00176| 00177| ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 00178| import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 00179| 00180| // Next.js 16 - turbopack at the top level of nextConfig 00181| const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 00182| turbopack: { 00183| // options 00184| }, 00185| } 00186| 00187| export default nextConfig 00188| ``` 00189| 00190| Make sure to review the `Turbopack` configuration [options](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack). **Next.js 16** introduces various improvements and new options, for example: 00191| 00192| - [Advanced Webpack loader conditions](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack#advanced-webpack-loader-conditions) 00193| - [debugIds](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack#debug-ids) 00194| 00195| ### Resolve alias fallback 00196| 00197| In some projects, client-side code may import files containing Node.js native modules. This will cause `Module not found: Can't resolve 'fs'` type of errors. 00198| 00199| When this happens, you should refactor your code so that your client-side bundles do not reference these Node.js native modules. 00200| 00201| However, in some cases, this might not be possible. In Webpack the `resolve.fallback` option was typically used to **silence** the error. Turbopack offers a similar option, using `turbopack.resolveAlias`. In this case, tell Turbopack to load an empty module when `fs` is requested for the browser. 00202| 00203| ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 00204| import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 00205| 00206| const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 00207| turbopack: { 00208| resolveAlias: { 00209| fs: { 00210| browser: './empty.ts', // We recommend to fix code imports before using this method 00211| }, 00212| }, 00213| }, 00214| } 00215| 00216| export default nextConfig 00217| ``` 00218| 00219| It is preferable to refactor your modules so that client code doesn't ever import from modules using Node.js native modules. 00220| 00221| ### Sass node_modules imports 00222| 00223| Turbopack fully supports importing Sass files from `node_modules`. Note that while Webpack allowed the legacy tilde (`~`) prefix, Turbopack does not support this syntax. 00224| 00225| In Webpack: 00226| 00227| ```scss filename="styles/globals.scss" 00228| @import '~bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css'; 00229| ``` 00230| 00231| In Turbopack: 00232| 00233| ```scss filename="styles/globals.scss" 00234| @import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css'; 00235| ``` 00236| 00237| If changing the imports is not possible, you can use `turbopack.resolveAlias`. For example: 00238| 00239| ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 00240| import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 00241| 00242| const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 00243| turbopack: { 00244| resolveAlias: { 00245| '~*': '*', 00246| }, 00247| }, 00248| } 00249| 00250| export default nextConfig 00251| ``` 00252| 00253| ### Turbopack File System Caching 00254| 00255| Turbopack stores compiler artifacts on disk between runs, for significantly faster compile times across restarts. Filesystem caching is enabled by default for both `next dev` and `next build`, through `experimental.turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev` and `experimental.turbopackFileSystemCacheForBuild`. See [Turbopack FileSystem Caching](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache) to configure or disable either one. 00256| 00257| 00258| 00259| ## Async Request APIs (Breaking change) 00260| 00261| Version 15 introduced [Async Request APIs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15#async-request-apis-breaking-change) as a breaking change, with **temporary** synchronous compatibility. 00262| 00263| Starting with **Next.js 16**, synchronous access is fully removed. These APIs can only be accessed asynchronously. 00264| 00265| - [`cookies`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies) 00266| - [`headers`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers) 00267| - [`draftMode`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/draft-mode) 00268| - `params` in [`layout.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout), [`page.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), [`route.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), [`default.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/default), [`opengraph-image`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/opengraph-image#opengraph-image), [`twitter-image`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/opengraph-image#twitter-image), [`icon`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/app-icons#icon), and [`apple-icon`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/app-icons#apple-icon). 00269| - `searchParams` in [`page.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page) 00270| 00271| Use the [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/codemods#migrate-to-async-dynamic-apis) to migrate to async Request-time APIs. 00272| 00273| ### Migrating types for async Request-time APIs 00274| 00275| To help migrate to async `params` and `searchParams`, you can run [`npx next typegen`](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#next-typegen-options) to automatically generate these globally available types helpers: 00276| 00277| - [`PageProps`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#page-props-helper) 00278| - [`LayoutProps`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout#layout-props-helper) 00279| - [`RouteContext`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route#route-context-helper) 00280| 00281| > **Good to know**: `typegen` was introduced in Next.js 15.5 00282| 00283| This simplifies type-safe migration to the new async API pattern, and enables you to update your components with full type safety, for example: 00284| 00285| ```tsx filename="/app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" 00286| export default async function Page(props: PageProps<'/blog/[slug]'>) { 00287| const { slug } = await props.params 00288| const query = await props.searchParams 00289| return

Blog Post: {slug}

00290| } 00291| ``` 00292| 00293| This approach gives you fully type-safe access to `props.params`, including the `slug`, and to `searchParams`, directly within your page. 00294| 00295| ## Async parameters for icon, and open-graph Image (Breaking change) 00296| 00297| > The props passed to the image generating functions in `opengraph-image`, `twitter-image`, `icon`, and `apple-icon`, are now Promises. 00298| 00299| In previous versions, both the `Image` (image generation function), and the `generateImageMetadata` received a `params` object. The `id` returned by `generateImageMetadata` was passed as a string to the image generation function. 00300| 00301| ```js filename="app/shop/[slug]/opengraph-image.js" 00302| // Next.js 15 - synchronous params access 00303| export function generateImageMetadata({ params }) { 00304| const { slug } = params 00305| return [{ id: '1' }, { id: '2' }] 00306| } 00307| 00308| // Next.js 15 - synchronous params and id access 00309| export default function Image({ params, id }) { 00310| const slug = params.slug 00311| const imageId = id // string 00312| // ... 00313| } 00314| ``` 00315| 00316| Starting with **Next.js 16**, to align with the [Async Request APIs](#async-request-apis-breaking-change) change, the image generating function now receives `params` and `id` as promises. The `generateImageMetadata` function continues to receive synchronous `params`. 00317| 00318| ```js filename="app/shop/[slug]/opengraph-image.js" 00319| export async function generateImageMetadata({ params }) { 00320| const { slug } = params 00321| return [{ id: '1' }, { id: '2' }] 00322| } 00323| 00324| // Next.js 16 - asynchronous params and id access 00325| export default async function Image({ params, id }) { 00326| const { slug } = await params // params now async 00327| const imageId = await id // id is now Promise when using generateImageMetadata 00328| // ... 00329| } 00330| ``` 00331| 00332| ## Async `id` parameter for `sitemap` (Breaking change) 00333| 00334| Previously, the `id` values returned from [`generateSitemaps`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-sitemaps) were passed directly to the `sitemap` generating function. 00335| 00336| ```js filename="app/product/sitemap.js" 00337| export async function generateSitemaps() { 00338| return [{ id: 0 }, { id: 1 }, { id: 2 }, { id: 3 }] 00339| } 00340| 00341| // Next.js 15 - synchronous id access 00342| export default async function sitemap({ id }) { 00343| const start = id * 50000 // id is a number 00344| // ... 00345| } 00346| ``` 00347| 00348| Starting with **Next.js 16**, the `sitemap` generating function now receives `id` as a promise. 00349| 00350| ```js filename="app/product/sitemap.js" 00351| export async function generateSitemaps() { 00352| return [{ id: 0 }, { id: 1 }, { id: 2 }, { id: 3 }] 00353| } 00354| 00355| // Next.js 16 - asynchronous id access 00356| export default async function sitemap({ id }) { 00357| const resolvedId = await id // id is now Promise 00358| const start = Number(resolvedId) * 50000 00359| // ... 00360| } 00361| ``` 00362| 00363| ## React 19.2 00364| 00365| The App Router in **Next.js 16** uses the latest React [Canary release](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries), which includes the newly released React 19.2 features and other features being incrementally stabilized. Highlights include: 00366| 00367| - **[View Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition)**: Animate elements that update inside a Transition or navigation 00368| - **[`useEffectEvent`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffectEvent)**: Extract non-reactive logic from Effects into reusable Effect Event functions 00369| - **[Activity](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity)**: Render "background activity" by hiding UI with `display: none` while maintaining state and cleaning up Effects 00370| 00371| Learn more in the [React 19.2 announcement](https://react.dev/blog/2025/10/01/react-19-2). 00372| 00373| 00374| 00375| ## React Compiler Support 00376| 00377| Built-in support for the React Compiler is now stable in **Next.js 16** following the React Compiler's 1.0 release. The React Compiler automatically memoizes components, reducing unnecessary re-renders with zero manual code changes. 00378| 00379| The `reactCompiler` configuration option has been promoted from `experimental` to stable. It is not enabled by default as we continue gathering build performance data across different application types. 00380| 00381| ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 00382| import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 00383| 00384| const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 00385| reactCompiler: true, 00386| } 00387| 00388| export default nextConfig 00389| ``` 00390| 00391| ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 00392| /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 00393| const nextConfig = { 00394| reactCompiler: true, 00395| } 00396| 00397| module.exports = nextConfig 00398| ``` 00399| 00400| Install the latest version of the React Compiler plugin: 00401| 00402| ```bash package="pnpm" 00403| pnpm add -D babel-plugin-react-compiler 00404| ``` 00405| 00406| ```bash package="npm" 00407| npm install -D babel-plugin-react-compiler 00408| ``` 00409| 00410| ```bash package="yarn" 00411| yarn add -D babel-plugin-react-compiler 00412| ``` 00413| 00414| ```bash package="bun" 00415| bun add -D babel-plugin-react-compiler 00416| ``` 00417| 00418| > **Good to know:** Expect compile times in development and during builds to be higher when enabling this option as the React Compiler relies on Babel. 00419| 00420| 00421| 00422| ## Caching APIs 00423| 00424| ### revalidateTag 00425| 00426| [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) now requires a second argument specifying a [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#reference) profile. The single-argument form is deprecated and will produce a TypeScript error. 00427| 00428| ```ts 00429| // Before 00430| revalidateTag('posts') 00431| 00432| // After 00433| revalidateTag('posts', 'max') 00434| ``` 00435| 00436| If you need immediate expiration rather than stale-while-revalidate, use [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag) in Server Actions instead. 00437| 00438| ```ts filename="app/actions.ts" switcher 00439| 'use server' 00440| 00441| import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache' 00442| 00443| export async function updateArticle(articleId: string) { 00444| // Mark article data as stale - article readers see stale data while it revalidates 00445| revalidateTag(`article-${articleId}`, 'max') 00446| } 00447| ``` 00448| 00449| ```js filename="app/actions.js" switcher 00450| 'use server' 00451| 00452| import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache' 00453| 00454| export async function updateArticle(articleId) { 00455| // Mark article data as stale - article readers see stale data while it revalidates 00456| revalidateTag(`article-${articleId}`, 'max') 00457| } 00458| ``` 00459| 00460| Use `revalidateTag` for content where a slight delay in updates is acceptable, such as blog posts, product catalogs, or documentation. Users receive stale content while fresh data loads in the background. 00461| 00462| ### updateTag 00463| 00464| [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag) is a new [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data#what-are-server-functions)-only API that provides **read-your-writes** semantics, where a user makes a change and the UI immediately shows the change, rather than stale data. 00465| 00466| It does this by expiring and immediately refreshing data within the same request. 00467| 00468| ```ts filename="app/actions.ts" switcher 00469| 'use server' 00470| 00471| import { updateTag } from 'next/cache' 00472| 00473| export async function updateUserProfile(userId: string, profile: Profile) { 00474| await db.users.update(userId, profile) 00475| 00476| // Expire cache and refresh immediately - user sees their changes right away 00477| updateTag(`user-${userId}`) 00478| } 00479| ``` 00480| 00481| ```js filename="app/actions.js" switcher 00482| 'use server' 00483| 00484| import { updateTag } from 'next/cache' 00485| 00486| export async function updateUserProfile(userId, profile) { 00487| await db.users.update(userId, profile) 00488| 00489| // Expire cache and refresh immediately - user sees their changes right away 00490| updateTag(`user-${userId}`) 00491| } 00492| ``` 00493| 00494| This ensures interactive features reflect changes immediately. Perfect for forms, user settings, and any workflow where users expect to see their updates instantly. 00495| 00496| Learn more about when to use `updateTag` or `revalidateTag` [here](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag#when-to-use-updatetag). 00497| 00498| ### refresh 00499| 00500| [`refresh`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/refresh) allows you to refresh the client router from within a Server Action. 00501| 00502| ```ts filename="app/actions.ts" switcher 00503| 'use server' 00504| 00505| import { refresh } from 'next/cache' 00506| 00507| export async function markNotificationAsRead(notificationId: string) { 00508| // Update the notification in the database 00509| await db.notifications.markAsRead(notificationId) 00510| 00511| // Refresh the notification count displayed in the header 00512| refresh() 00513| } 00514| ``` 00515| 00516| ```js filename="app/actions.js" switcher 00517| 'use server' 00518| 00519| import { refresh } from 'next/cache' 00520| 00521| export async function markNotificationAsRead(notificationId) { 00522| // Update the notification in the database 00523| await db.notifications.markAsRead(notificationId) 00524| 00525| // Refresh the notification count displayed in the header 00526| refresh() 00527| } 00528| ``` 00529| 00530| Use it when you need to refresh the client router after performing an action. 00531| 00532| ### cacheLife and cacheTag 00533| 00534| [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) and [`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) are now stable. The `unstable_` prefix is no longer needed. 00535| 00536| Wherever you had aliased imports like: 00537| 00538| ```ts 00539| import { 00540| unstable_cacheLife as cacheLife, 00541| unstable_cacheTag as cacheTag, 00542| } from 'next/cache' 00543| ``` 00544| 00545| You can update your imports to: 00546| 00547| ```ts 00548| import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache' 00549| ``` 00550| 00551| ## Enhanced Routing and Navigation 00552| 00553| **Next.js 16** includes a complete overhaul of the routing and navigation system, making page transitions leaner and faster. This optimizes how Next.js prefetches and caches navigation data: 00554| 00555| - **Layout deduplication**: When prefetching multiple URLs with a shared layout, the layout is downloaded once. 00556| - **Incremental prefetching**: Next.js only prefetches parts not already in cache, rather than entire pages. 00557| 00558| These changes require **no code modifications** and are designed to improve performance across all apps. 00559| 00560| However, you may see more individual prefetch requests with much lower total transfer sizes. We believe this is the right trade-off for nearly all applications. 00561| 00562| If the increased request count causes issues, please let us know by creating an [issue](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues) or [discussion](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions) item. 00563| 00564| ## Partial Prerendering (PPR) 00565| 00566| **Next.js 16** removes the experimental **Partial Prerendering (PPR)** flag and configuration options, including the route level segment `experimental_ppr`. 00567| 00568| Starting with **Next.js 16**, you can opt into PPR using the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) configuration. 00569| 00570| ```js filename="next.config.js" 00571| /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 00572| const nextConfig = { 00573| cacheComponents: true, 00574| } 00575| 00576| module.exports = nextConfig 00577| ``` 00578| 00579| PPR in **Next.js 16** works differently than in **Next.js 15** canaries. If you are using PPR today, stay in the current Next.js 15 canary you are using. See [Migrating to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components) for migration patterns. 00580| 00581| ```js filename="next.config.js" 00582| /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 00583| const nextConfig = { 00584| // If you are using PPR today 00585| // stay in the current Next.js 15 canary 00586| experimental: { 00587| ppr: true, 00588| }, 00589| } 00590| 00591| module.exports = nextConfig 00592| ``` 00593| 00594| 00595| 00596| ## `middleware` to `proxy` 00597| 00598| The `middleware` filename is deprecated, and has been renamed to `proxy` to clarify network boundary and routing focus. 00599| 00600| The `edge` runtime is **NOT** supported in `proxy`. The `proxy` runtime is `nodejs`, and it cannot be configured. If you want to continue using the `edge` runtime, keep using `middleware`. title: How to upgrade to version 16

description: Upgrade your Next.js Application from Version 15 to 16.

{/* The content of this doc is shared between the app and pages router. You can use the `<PagesOnly>Content</PagesOnly>` component to add content that is specific to the Pages Router. Any shared content should not be wrapped in a component. */}

## Use a coding agent (recommended)

Run the latest upgrade CLI from your app's directory:

```bash filename="Terminal"
npx next@canary upgrade --agent=latest
```

The CLI prepares the Next.js 16 migration guides and codemod command for the agent, then asks it to apply the changes and verify the app. See [Upgrade with a coding agent](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/agent-upgrade) for details.

00087|   Continue with Claude Code
00088|   Copy prompt for another coding agent
00089|   Cancel
00090| 
00091| Which Codex model should run the upgrade?
00092| ❯ Terra
00093|   Sol
00094|   Cancel
00095| 
00096| Which reasoning effort should the upgrade use?
00097|   low
00098|   medium
00099| ❯ high
00100|   xhigh
00101|   max
00102|   ultra
00103|   Cancel

00106| ❯ Yes

00108|   Cancel
00109|

00111| ❯ Yes

title: Caching
description: Learn how to cache data and UI in Next.js
related:
  title: Next Steps
  description: Learn more about revalidation and the APIs mentioned on this page.
  links:
    - app/getting-started/revalidating
    - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache

    - app/guides/instant-navigation
---

> This page covers caching with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. If you're not using Cache Components, see the [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components) guide.

Caching is a technique for storing the result of data fetching and other computations so that future requests for the same data can be served faster, without doing the work again.

## Enabling Cache Components

New App Router apps created with the recommended [`create-next-app`](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/create-next-app) defaults already have Cache Components and Partial Prefetching enabled.

> This page covers caching with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. If you're not using Cache Components, see the [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components) guide.

Caching is a technique for storing the result of data fetching and other computations so that future requests for the same data can be served faster, without doing the work again.

## Enabling Cache Components

New App Router apps created with the recommended [`create-next-app`](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/create-next-app) defaults already have Cache Components and Partial Prefetching enabled.
